acrocanthosaurus:eswiki:9.title: Acrocanthosaurus atokensis (Cerebro y estructura interna del oído)

facts.statement: The genus Acrocanthosaurus was named and described by American paleontologists Stovall and Langston in 1950.
facts.quote: authority: Stovall & Langston, 1950

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous (Barremian) and Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian) periods.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Cretaceous to Late Cretaceous (Barremian to Cenomanian)

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus existed between 125 and 99.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: from 125 to 99.6 million years ago

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus is characterized by high neural spines on its vertebrae that likely supported a large muscle ridge along its neck, back, and hips.
facts.quote: As the name suggests, it is best known for the high neural spines on many of its vertebrae, which most likely supported a ridge of muscle over the animal's neck, back, and hips

facts.statement: The largest known specimen of Acrocanthosaurus measured 11 to 11.5 meters in length and weighed between 4.4 and 8.4 metric tons.
facts.quote: with the largest known specimen reaching 11 - 11.5 m in length and 4.4 and 8.4 MT in weight

facts.statement: The name Acrocanthosaurus was coined in 1950 by J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston Jr.
facts.quote: The name was coined in 1950 by American paleontologists J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston Jr

facts.statement: The species name atokensis refers to Atoka County in Oklahoma, where the original specimens were discovered.
facts.quote: The lone named species (A. atokensis), is after Atoka County in Oklahoma, where the original specimens were found

facts.statement: The holotype and paratype specimens of Acrocanthosaurus were discovered in the early 1940s and formally described in 1950.
facts.quote: The holotype and paratype (OMNH 10146 and OMNH 10147), discovered in the early 1940s and described at the same time in 1950

facts.statement: A highly complete skeleton nicknamed "Fran" was recovered from the Antlers Formation of Oklahoma by Cephis Hall and Sid Love.
facts.quote: An even more complete skeleton (NCSM 14345, nicknamed "Fran") was recovered from the Antlers Formation of Oklahoma by Cephis Hall and Sid Love

facts.statement: The presence of Acrocanthosaurus in the Cloverly Formation was established in 2012 with the description of specimen UM 20796.
facts.quote: The presence of Acrocanthosaurus in the Cloverly Formation was established in 2012 with the description of another partial skeleton (UM 20796)

facts.statement: In 2024, an incomplete skeleton from the Arundel Formation was identified as a subadult Acrocanthosaurus, marking the first definitive record from eastern North America.
facts.quote: In 2024, an incomplete theropod skeleton (USNM 466054) from the Arundel Formation was identified as that of a subadult Acrocanthosaurus

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus had an estimated skull length of 1.23 to 1.29 meters and a body length of 11 to 12 meters.
facts.quote: with an estimated skull length of 1.23 - 1.29 m and body length of 11 - 12 m

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus had nineteen curved, serrated teeth on each side of its upper jaw.
facts.quote: Nineteen curved, serrated teeth lined each side of the upper jaw

facts.statement: Large theropod footprints found in Texas may belong to Acrocanthosaurus, though no direct link to skeletal remains has been confirmed.
facts.quote: Large theropod footprints discovered in Texas may have been made by Acrocanthosaurus, although no direct association with skeletal remains has been found

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus had a continent-wide range across North America, with fossils found in Arizona, Oklahoma, Texas, Utah, Wyoming, and Maryland.
facts.quote: It had a continent-wide range, with fossil remains known from the U.S. states of Arizona, Oklahoma, Texas, Utah, and Wyoming in the west and Maryland in the east

facts.statement: The lower spines of Acrocanthosaurus attached powerful muscles similar to modern bison, likely forming a tall, thick ridge along its back.
facts.quote: The lower spines of Acrocanthosaurus had attachments for powerful muscles like those of modern bison, probably forming a tall, thick ridge down its back.

facts.statement: The function of Acrocanthosaurus's tall spines is unknown, though researchers suggest they may have been used for communication, fat storage, muscle attachment, or temperature control.
facts.quote: The function of the spines remains unknown, although they may have been involved in communication, fat storage, muscle, or temperature control.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus had shorter and more robust forelimbs than Allosaurus, with each hand bearing three clawed digits.
facts.quote: Its forelimbs were relatively shorter and more robust than those of Allosaurus but were otherwise similar: each hand bore three clawed digits.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus had four digits on each foot, with the first digit being much smaller and not touching the ground.
facts.quote: Its feet had four digits each, although, as is typical for theropods, the first was much smaller than the rest and did not make contact with the ground.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus is classified within the superfamily Allosauroidea and the infraorder Tetanurae.
facts.quote: Acrocanthosaurus is classified in the superfamily Allosauroidea within the infraorder Tetanurae.

facts.statement: Most studies classify Acrocanthosaurus as a member of the family Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: Most studies have found it to be a member of the related family Carcharodontosauridae.

facts.statement: J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston Jr. first assigned Acrocanthosaurus to Antrodemidae, but Alfred Sherwood Romer transferred it to the wastebasket taxon Megalosauridae in 1956.
facts.quote: J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston Jr. first assigned it to the "Antrodemidae", the equivalent of the Allosauridae, but it was transferred to the Megalosauridae, a wastebasket taxon, by Alfred Sherwood Romer in 1956.

facts.statement: In 1988, Gregory S. Paul named a second species, A. altispinax, based on tall spined vertebrae from the Early Cretaceous of England that were once thought similar to Acrocanthosaurus.
facts.quote: Tall spined vertebrae from the Early Cretaceous of England were once considered to be very similar to those of Acrocanthosaurus, and in 1988 Gregory S. Paul named them as a second species of the genus, A. altispinax.

facts.statement: When accounting for lost Harris lines, Acrocanthosaurus likely needed 18 to 24 years to reach maturity.
facts.quote: If accounting for these lines, then Acrocanthosaurus needed 18–24 years to be mature.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus had a powerful bite, with an anterior force of 8,266 newtons and a posterior force of 16,894 newtons.
facts.quote: According to the results, its bite force at the anterior part of the jaws was 8,266 newtons, while the posterior bite force was estimated to be 16,894 newtons.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that differences between specimens may indicate a need to reexamine North American carcharodontosaurid material, potentially revealing greater diversity than previously thought.
facts.quote: While beyond the scope of their paper, the authors note that these differences may be grounds for a reexamination of North American carcharodontosaurid material, and may suggest a much richer diversity than once thought.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus forelimbs did not touch the ground and were used for hunting rather than walking.
facts.quote: Like those of most other non-avian theropods, Acrocanthosaurus forelimbs did not make contact with the ground and were not used for locomotion; instead, they served a predatory function.

facts.statement: The Acrocanthosaurus arm could not reach a vertical position when swinging down but could swing up to 9 degrees above horizontal.
facts.quote: The arm was unable to reach a vertical position when adducting (swinging downwards) but could abduct (swing upwards) to 9° above horizontal.

facts.statement: The Acrocanthosaurus forearm bones locked together, preventing the twisting motion seen in human forearms.
facts.quote: The radius and ulna (forearm bones) locked together so that there was no possibility of pronation or supination (twisting) as in human forearms.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus forelimbs were likely not used to initially capture prey, suggesting the animal hunted by leading with its mouth.
facts.quote: Therefore, they were not likely to have been used in the initial capture of prey and Acrocanthosaurus probably led with its mouth when hunting.

facts.statement: After seizing prey, Acrocanthosaurus likely retracted its heavily muscled forelimbs to hold the prey tightly against its body.
facts.quote: Once prey had been seized in the jaws, the heavily muscled forelimbs may have retracted, holding the prey tightly against the body and preventing escape.

facts.statement: The extreme ability of Acrocanthosaurus digits to bend backward may have been an adaptation to hold struggling prey without dislocation.
facts.quote: The extreme hyperextensibility of the digits may have been an adaptation allowing Acrocanthosaurus to hold struggling prey without fear of dislocation.

facts.statement: One theory suggests Acrocanthosaurus held prey in its jaws while retracting its forelimbs to tear large gashes with its claws.
facts.quote: Another possibility is that Acrocanthosaurus held its prey in its jaws, while repeatedly retracting its forelimbs, tearing large gashes with its claws.

facts.statement: The Acrocanthosaurus brain was most similar to that of allosauroids rather than other theropods.
facts.quote: While the brain is similar to many theropods, it is most similar to that of allosauroids.

facts.statement: The Acrocanthosaurus brain resembles those of Carcharodontosaurus and Giganotosaurus, supporting the hypothesis that it was a carcharodontosaurid.
facts.quote: It most resembles the brains of Carcharodontosaurus and Giganotosaurus rather than those of Allosaurus or Sinraptor, providing support for the hypothesis that Acrocanthosaurus was a carcharodontosaurid.

facts.statement: Reconstruction of the Acrocanthosaurus ear suggests its head was held at a 25-degree angle below horizontal.
facts.quote: Reconstructing the semicircular canals of the ear, which control balance, shows that the head was held at a 25° angle below horizontal.

facts.statement: The Glen Rose Formation in central Texas preserves many large, three-toed theropod footprints.
facts.quote: The Glen Rose Formation of central Texas preserves many dinosaur footprints, including large, three-toed theropod prints.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the Glen Rose trackways represent a pack of Acrocanthosaurus stalking sauropods, as other explanations exist and the hypothesis is difficult to prove.
facts.quote: This has been put forth as evidence that a small pack of Acrocanthosaurus was stalking a herd of sauropods. While interesting and plausible, this hypothesis is difficult to prove and other explanations exist.

facts.statement: The Acrocanthosaurus holotype had a fractured and healed neural spine on the eleventh vertebra and an unusual hook-like structure on the third tail vertebra.
facts.quote: The neural spine of the eleventh vertebra was fractured and healed while the neural spine of its third tail vertebra had an unusual hook-like structure.

facts.statement: The environment where Acrocanthosaurus fossils were found was a large floodplain draining into a shallow inland sea.
facts.quote: During this time, the area preserved in the Twin Mountains and Antlers formations was a large floodplain that drained into a shallow inland sea.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus spread across North America before the Western Interior Seaway expanded to divide the continent.
facts.quote: The presence of Acrocanthosaurus in the Arundel Formation suggests that it had managed to spread across the continent before the seaway could impede it.

facts.statement: Definite Acrocanthosaurus fossils have been found in formations across Texas, Oklahoma, Wyoming, Arizona, Utah, and Maryland.
facts.quote: Definite Acrocanthosaurus fossils have been found in the Twin Mountains Formation of northern Texas, the Antlers Formation of southern Oklahoma, the Cloverly Formation of north-central Wyoming, the Turney Ranch Formation of Arizona, Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah and the Arundel Formation in Maryland.

facts.statement: Fossils of Acrocanthosaurus have been found in Oklahoma and Texas, with teeth attributed to the genus found in Maryland.
facts.quote: Sus restos fósiles han sido hallados en los estados de Oklahoma y Texas, mientras que dientes atribuidos a este género proceden de Maryland.

facts.statement: Large fossil footprints found in Texas may belong to Acrocanthosaurus, though they have not been directly linked to skeletons.
facts.quote: Grandes huellas fósiles descubiertas en Texas pudieron pertenecer al acrocantosaurio, aunque no se las ha asociado directamente con esqueletos.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus was a bipedal predator known for high neural spines on its vertebrae that likely supported a hump over its neck, back, and hips.
facts.quote: El Acrocanthosaurus era un depredador bípedo, y como el nombre indica, se lo conoce principalmente por sus apófisis espinosa, ubicadas en muchas de sus vértebras, y que parecen haber sostenido una «joroba» encima del cuello, espalda y caderas del animal.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus was one of the largest theropods, reaching nearly 12 meters in length and weighing between 5.7 and 6.2 tonnes.
facts.quote: El acrocantosaurio fue uno de los terópodos más grandes, de casi 12 metros de longitud y un peso de entre 5.7 a 6.2 toneladas.

facts.statement: The largest and most complete individual, NCSM 14345, is estimated to be 11.5 meters long, weigh between 5.7 and 6.2 tonnes (with a possible maximum of 7.25 tonnes), and have a skull about 1.3 meters long.
facts.quote: El individuo más grande y completo que se ha descubierto, NCSM 14345 se estima que su longitud fue de 11,5 metros y con un peso estimado de 5,7 a 6,2 toneladas, con un rango máximo de 7,25 toneladas posibles para el espécimen y su cráneo medía aproximadamente 1,3 metros de largo.

facts.statement: The most distinctive feature of Acrocanthosaurus is a row of high neural spines running from the neck to the end of the tail, measuring up to 2.5 times the height of the vertebra.
facts.quote: Lo que más destaca al acrocantosaurio es su fila de altas espinas neurales que se localizan en las vértebras desde el cuello hasta el final de la cola, midiendo hasta 2,5 veces la altura de la vértebra.

facts.statement: The function of the high spines is unknown, though they likely served for communication, fat storage, or thermoregulation.
facts.quote: La función de estas espinas permanece desconocida, aunque probablemente pudieron servir para la comunicación, almacenamiento de grasa, o termorregulación.

facts.statement: Unlike many smaller, fast dinosaurs, the femur was longer than the tibia and metatarsus, indicating Acrocanthosaurus was not a fast runner.
facts.quote: A diferencia de muchos dinosaurios veloces más pequeños, el fémur era más largo que la tibia y el metatarso, demostrando que el acrocantosaurio no era un rápido corredor.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus is classified within the family Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Carcharodontosauridae

facts.statement: The genus Acrocanthosaurus was named by Stovall and Langston in 1950.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Stovall & Langston, 1950

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate regarding Acrocanthosaurus's evolutionary relationships, with some scientists classifying it as an allosaurid and others as a carcharodontosaurid.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, persiste el debate sobre sus relaciones evolutivas, mientras que algunos científicos lo clasifican como un alosáurido, otros en cambio sostienen que es un carcarodontosáurido.

facts.statement: The genus name Acrocanthosaurus means 'high-spine lizard' and refers to the animal's high neural spines.
facts.quote: Acrocanthosaurus fue nombrado por sus altas espinas neurales, del griego ακρα/akra ("alta"), ακανθα/akantha ("espina") y σαυρος/sauros ("lagarto").

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus was formally named in 1950 by American paleontologists J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston, Jr.
facts.quote: El nombre fue acuñado en 1950 por los paleontólogos estadounidenses J. Willis Stovall y Wann Langston, Jr.

facts.statement: Only one species, A. atokensis, is described, named after Atoka County, Oklahoma, where the first specimens were found.
facts.quote: Solo hay una especie descrita (A. atokensis), nombrada por el condado de Atoka en Oklahoma, donde los primeros especímenes fueron encontrados.

facts.statement: The holotype and paratype specimens were discovered in the early 1940s and described together in 1950.
facts.quote: El holotipo y paratipo, OMNH 10146 y OMNH 10147 respectivamente, fueron descubiertos a principios de la década de 1940 y descritos al mismo tiempo en 1950

facts.statement: The most complete skeleton, nicknamed 'Fran' (specimen NCSM 14345), was found by private collectors in the Antlers Formation.
facts.quote: El más completo de los esqueletos, NCSM 14345, apodado «Fran», fue hallado también en la Formación de Antlers por coleccionistas privados

facts.statement: The presence of Acrocanthosaurus in the Cloverly Formation was established in 2012 with the description of partial skeleton UM 20796.
facts.quote: La presencia de Acrocanthosaurus en la Formación Cloverly se estableció en 2012 con la descripción de otro esqueleto parcial, UM 20796.

facts.statement: Teeth from the Arundel Formation in Maryland suggest Acrocanthosaurus may have ranged as far east as eastern North America.
facts.quote: Varios dientes de la Formación de Arundel en Maryland han sido identificados con los del acrocantosaurio e indican una posible distribución hasta el extremo este de Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Brain reconstruction supports the hypothesis that Acrocanthosaurus was a carcharodontosaurid, showing similarities to Allosaurus and Sinraptor rather than other theropods.
facts.quote: Así se demostró que el cerebro es parecido al de muchos otros terópodos, pero guarda más semejanza con el de los alosauroides tales como el carcarodontosaurio y el giganotosaurio, y no con los del alosaurio y del sinraptor, siendo soporte para la hipótesis de que el acrocantosaurio fue un carcarodontosáurido.

facts.statement: Like non-avian theropods, Acrocanthosaurus arms did not touch the ground and were used for hunting rather than locomotion.
facts.quote: Como otros terópodos no-avianos, los brazos del acrocantosaurio no tocaban el suelo y no se usaban para la locomoción, sirviendo en cambio para la caza.

facts.statement: The shoulder had a limited range of motion, allowing the arm to retract 109 degrees from the vertical but not make a full circle.
facts.quote: El hombro del acrocantosaurio poseía un rango de movimiento menor que el de los humanos. Los brazos no podían hacer un círculo completo pero podía retraerlo 109° grados de la línea vertical.

facts.statement: Elbow movement was limited to a total range of only 57 degrees compared to humans.
facts.quote: El movimiento del codo también fue limitado comparado a los seres humanos, con una amplitud total de movimiento de solamente 57.º

facts.statement: Although arms were used for hunting, they could not open wide enough to grab prey by the neck.
facts.quote: Antes del estudio de los miembros delanteros se suponía que eran usados para la caza, pero estos no podían abrirse lo suficiente como para atrapar el cuello de su presa.

facts.statement: Once prey was pinned against the body, Acrocanthosaurus likely killed it with bites.
facts.quote: Una vez con la presa atrapada contra el cuerpo, el acrocantosaurio podría haberla matado a dentelladas.

facts.statement: Large olfactory bulbs indicate Acrocanthosaurus had a keen sense of smell.
facts.quote: El acrocantosaurio poseía grandes bulbos olfativos que indican un buen sentido del olfato.

facts.statement: Ear canal reconstruction suggests the head was held at a horizontal angle of less than 25 degrees when alert.
facts.quote: Al reconstruirse los canales semicirculares del oído, los cuales controlan el equilibrio, demuestran que la cabeza se mantenía a un ángulo horizontal debajo de los 25.º

facts.statement: The holotype skull shows a slight exostosis on the squamosal bone.
facts.quote: El cráneo del holotipo de Acrocanthosaurus atokensis muestra una ligera exostosis en el material de la escamoso.

facts.statement: The eleventh neural spine was fractured and healed, while the third tail neural spine had an unusual hook-like structure.
facts.quote: La espina neural de la undécima vértebra estuvo fracturada y terminó sanando, mientras que la espina neural de la tercera vértebra de su cola tenía una inusual estructura en forma de gancho.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus lived from the Aptian to Cenomanian stages, between 121.4 and 93.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Cenomanian (121.4 to 93.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: A juvenile specimen was found in a bone bed in the Bighorn Basin, Wyoming, near the shoulder blade of a Sauroposeidon.
facts.quote: Proviene de una cama de huesos en la cuenca Bighorn del centro-norte de Wyoming, y fue encontrado cerca del omóplato de un Sauroposeidon.

facts.statement: Many fossils previously assigned to Acrocanthosaurus from the western US are now under debate following the description of specimens in the Cloverly Formation.
facts.quote: Muchos otros dientes y huesos, procedentes de varias formaciones geológicas alrededor del oeste estadounidense, se han asignado a Acrocanthosaurus, pero muchos han sido identificados erróneamente. Sin embargo esto ha sido puesto en discusión después de la descripción de ejemplares en la formación Clovery.
